title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: When I was seventeen, my parents decided I should attend the university at Ingolstadt. I'd been educated in Geneva's schools until then, but my father thought that, to complete my education, I needed to get to know customs other than those of my own country. My departure was set for an early date. But before that day could arrive, the first misfortune of my life struck — an omen, as it were, of the misery to come.

Elizabeth had caught scarlet fever. Her illness was severe, and she was in the greatest danger. Many arguments were made to persuade my mother not to nurse her. She yielded to our pleas at first. But when she heard that Elizabeth's life was threatened, she could no longer control her anxiety. She went to the sickbed. Her devoted care triumphed over the disease — Elizabeth was saved. But the consequences of this rashness were fatal for her rescuer. On the third day, my mother fell ill. Her fever came with the most alarming symptoms. Her doctors' faces predicted the worst. On her deathbed, the courage and kindness of this best of women did not desert her. She joined Elizabeth's hand with mine. "My children," she said, "my greatest hope for future happiness was the prospect of your union. This will now be your father's consolation. Elizabeth, my love, you must take my place with the younger children. Alas! I'm sorry to be taken from you. Happy and beloved as I've been, it's hard to leave you all. But these aren't fitting thoughts. I'll try to accept death cheerfully and hold onto the hope of meeting you in another world."

She died peacefully. Her face expressed love even in death. I don't need to describe the feelings of those whose dearest bonds are torn apart by that most irreparable evil — the void it leaves in the soul, the despair written on every face. It takes so long for the mind to accept that someone we saw every day, whose very existence seemed part of our own, is gone forever — that the brightness of a beloved eye has been extinguished and a voice so familiar and dear will never be heard again. These are the thoughts of the first days. But when time confirms the reality of the loss, the true bitterness of grief begins. Yet who hasn't had someone dear torn away? Why should I describe a sorrow everyone has felt and must feel? Eventually, grief becomes more of an indulgence than a necessity. The smile that plays on the lips, though it might seem like a sacrilege, is not banished. My mother was dead, but we still had duties to fulfill. We had to continue our lives and learn to count ourselves fortunate as long as even one of us remained whom death, the great plunderer, had not seized.

My departure for Ingolstadt, delayed by these events, was now set again. I obtained a few weeks' reprieve from my father. It felt like sacrilege to leave the quiet, death-like atmosphere of our mourning house so soon and rush into the thick of life. Grief was new to me, but no less frightening for that. I was reluctant to leave those who remained, and above all, I wanted to see my sweet Elizabeth find some comfort.

She hid her grief and tried to comfort us all. She looked steadily at life and took up its duties with courage and determination. She devoted herself to those she'd been taught to call her uncle and cousins. She'd never been more captivating than during this time, when she called back the sunshine of her smiles and spent them on us. She forgot her own sorrow in her efforts to make us forget ours.

The day of my departure finally arrived. Clerval spent the last evening with us. He'd tried to persuade his father to let him come with me as a fellow student, but without success. His father was a narrow-minded tradesman who saw only idleness and ruin in his son's ambitions. Henry felt the misfortune of being denied a liberal education deeply. He said little, but when he spoke, I could read in his bright eyes and animated expression a restrained but firm resolve not to be chained to the petty details of commerce.

We stayed up late. We couldn't tear ourselves away from each other or bring ourselves to say "farewell." It was finally said, and we went to bed pretending to seek rest, each believing the other was fooled. But when I came down to the carriage at dawn, they were all there — my father to bless me once more, Clerval to press my hand one last time, Elizabeth to renew her pleas that I write often and to give her last tender attentions to her friend and playmate.

I threw myself into the carriage and gave in to the most melancholy thoughts. I, who had always been surrounded by loving companions, constantly trying to make each other happy — I was now alone. At the university I would have to make my own friends and be my own protector. My life had been remarkably sheltered and domestic, which gave me a deep resistance to new faces. I loved my brothers, Elizabeth, and Clerval — these were my "old familiar faces." I believed myself totally unfit for the company of strangers. These were my thoughts as I began my journey. But as I went on, my spirits and hopes rose. I deeply wanted knowledge. I'd often thought it hard to spend my youth confined to one place and had longed to enter the world and take my place among other people. Now my wishes were being fulfilled. It would have been foolish to regret it.

I had plenty of time for these and many other reflections during the long, tiring journey to Ingolstadt. At last the town's tall white steeple came into view. I got out and was taken to my solitary lodgings to spend the evening as I wished.

The next morning I delivered my letters of introduction and visited some of the chief professors. Chance — or rather the evil influence, the Angel of Destruction, which took all-powerful control of me from the moment I turned my reluctant steps away from my father's door — led me first to Professor Krempe, who taught natural philosophy. He was a rough man, but deeply versed in his science. He asked me several questions about my progress in various branches of natural science. I answered carelessly and, partly out of contempt, mentioned the names of my alchemist authors as the main writers I'd studied. The professor stared. "Have you," he said, "really spent your time studying such nonsense?"

I said I had. "Every minute," Professor Krempe continued with heat, "every instant you wasted on those books is utterly and entirely lost. You've stuffed your memory with discredited theories and worthless names. Good God! What desert did you grow up in, where no one was kind enough to tell you that these ideas you so eagerly absorbed are a thousand years old and as stale as they are ancient? In this age of science and enlightenment, I hardly expected to find a follower of Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus. My dear sir, you must begin your studies entirely from scratch."

With that, he stepped aside and wrote a list of books on natural philosophy for me to buy. He dismissed me after mentioning that the following week he'd begin a lecture course on natural philosophy in general, and that Professor Waldman, a colleague, would lecture on chemistry on alternate days.

I went home not disappointed, for as I've said, I had long considered the authors the professor condemned to be useless. But I was no more inclined to return to those studies in any form. Professor Krempe was a short, squat man with a harsh voice and unpleasant face. The teacher didn't endear me to his subject. Perhaps I have described too philosophically and too neatly the conclusions I had come to about these studies in my early years. As a child, I wasn't satisfied with what modern scientists promised. In my confusion — understandable given my youth and lack of guidance — I'd retraced the path of knowledge backward through time, exchanging modern discoveries for the dreams of forgotten alchemists. Besides, I had contempt for the goals of modern natural science. When the old masters sought immortality and power, their aims were grand, even if futile. But now everything had changed. Modern scientists seemed content to demolish the very visions that had first drawn me to science. I was being asked to trade boundless dreams for trivial realities.

These were my thoughts during my first few days at Ingolstadt, which I spent mostly getting to know the place and its residents. But as the following week began, I thought about what Professor Krempe had said about the lectures. I couldn't bring myself to go hear that smug little man hold forth from a lectern. But I remembered what he'd said about Professor Waldman, whom I hadn't met since he'd been away.

Partly from curiosity and partly from having nothing better to do, I went to the lecture hall. Professor Waldman entered shortly after. He was nothing like his colleague. He appeared about fifty years old, with a face full of kindness. A few gray hairs covered his temples, but those at the back were nearly black. He was short but remarkably upright, and his voice was the sweetest I'd ever heard. He began with a survey of the history of chemistry and the contributions of various scholars, speaking the names of the greatest discoverers with genuine passion. Then he gave an overview of the current state of the science and explained many of its basic concepts. After a few demonstrations, he concluded with a tribute to modern chemistry that I shall never forget:

"The ancient teachers of this science," he said, "promised impossible things and accomplished nothing. The modern masters promise very little. They know that metals can't be turned into gold and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. But these scientists, whose hands seem made only to dabble in dirt, and their eyes only to pore over the microscope or the crucible, have truly performed miracles. They penetrate into nature's inner workings and reveal how she operates in her most hidden places. They reach into the heavens. They've discovered how blood circulates and what the air we breathe is made of. They've gained new and nearly unlimited powers. They can command the lightning, mimic the earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with its own shadows."

Those were the professor's words — or rather, let me say, the words of fate — spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as if my soul were wrestling with an enemy I could touch. One by one, various keys were touched that formed the mechanism of my being. String after string was struck. Soon my mind was filled with one thought, one vision, one purpose. So much has been done, cried the soul of Frankenstein — more, far more, will I achieve. Following in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

I didn't close my eyes that night. My mind was in a state of upheaval and turmoil. I sensed that order would emerge from the chaos, but I had no power to make it happen. Gradually, after dawn, sleep came. When I woke, the previous night's thoughts felt like a dream. Only a resolution remained: to return to my old studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. That same day I visited Professor Waldman. His manner in private was even more warm and inviting than in public. The certain dignity he carried in the lecture hall was replaced at home by the greatest friendliness and kindness. I gave him roughly the same account of my former studies as I'd given his colleague. He listened attentively and smiled at the names of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus — but without Professor Krempe's contempt. He said, "These were men to whose tireless dedication modern scientists owe most of the foundations of their knowledge. They left us the easier task of giving new names and organizing the facts they were largely responsible for bringing to light. The work of brilliant minds, however wrongly directed, almost always ends up benefiting humanity." I listened to this fair, unpretentious statement, then told him his lecture had removed my prejudice against modern chemistry. I spoke carefully, with the modesty a young student owes his teacher, and let none of the enthusiasm driving my intended work slip out — my inexperience of life would have made me ashamed to. I asked his advice about which books to get.

"I'm happy," said Professor Waldman, "to have gained a student. If your effort matches your ability, I have no doubt you'll succeed. Chemistry is the branch of natural science where the greatest advances have been and may yet be made, which is why I've made it my specialty. But at the same time, I haven't neglected the other branches. A man who studied only chemistry would make a poor chemist. If you truly want to become a scientist and not merely a petty experimenter, I'd advise you to study every branch of natural philosophy, including mathematics."

He then took me into his laboratory and explained his various instruments. He told me what I should buy and promised I could use his own equipment once I'd advanced far enough not to damage it. He also gave me the book list I'd requested, and I took my leave.
So ended a day that was to be memorable for me. It decided my future destiny.
